concept.name: Closing auction
concept.definition: The call auction that establishes a security's official closing price at the end of regular trading, pooling market-on-close, limit-on-close, and continuous-book interest into a single-price cross.
concept.intuition: One final batch trade sets the closing print that indexes, funds, and performance reports all use as the day's price.
concept.mechanics: On Nasdaq, on-close orders are accepted until cutoffs (MOC by 3:55 p.m. ET, LOC by 3:58 p.m.), imbalance information is disseminated from 3:55 p.m., and at 4:00 p.m. the closing book and continuous book are crossed at the price that maximizes matched shares; the result sets the Nasdaq Official Closing Price and is distributed to the consolidated tape.
concept.failure_modes: Because index funds and benchmarks key off the close, the closing auction attracts enormous, sometimes one-sided volume; large imbalances can move the closing print away from the preceding continuous-market price.
concept.misconceptions: The closing price is not 'the last trade of the day' by definition — it is the price of the closing cross, which may differ from the final continuous-market trade and can be amended by clearly erroneous trade rules.
concept.example: On index rebalance day, hundreds of millions of shares route to closing auctions; a stock with a large sell imbalance closes at a cross price below its 3:59 p.m. continuous-market quote.

citations.source: Nasdaq, The Nasdaq Opening and Closing Crosses FAQ
